newsitem.title: TUNISIA: Only Libyan planes to fly pilgrims to Saudi, JANA.
newsitem.headline: Only Libyan planes to fly pilgrims to Saudi, JANA.

text.p: Libyan pilgrims to Saudi Arabia for the annual pilgrimage to Mecca would only fly this year aboard Libyan airlines despite a United Nations Security Council ban, the official Libyan news agency JANA reported on Thursday.
JANA, monitored in Tunis, also rejected that the Egyptian national carrier EgyptAir flies the Libyan pilgrims as it did over the past few years under a Security Council permission.

"It is unlawful to (get) permission from the Security Council on the haj because the issue is related to the core of the Moslem religious faith and is not a political issue for the Security Council or anyone else to rule on it," JANA's Arab Affairs commentator said.
"Therefore, it is the right of the Libyan pilgrims to make pilgrimage aboard Libyan airlines and any other airliner must not expect that it will carry Libyan pilgrims...," he added.

The United Nations has banned flights to and from Libya since 1992 as part of sanctions against Tripoli for failing to hand over for trial in the United States or Britain two Libyans suspected of blowing up an American airliner over the Scottish town of Lockerbie in December 1988.

Egyptian government newspapers on Tuesday reported that the U.N. sanctions committee, entitled to waive the ban in special cases, has given EgyptAir permission to fly 11,000 Libyan pilgrims to Saudi Arabia.
EgyptAir will make 90 return flights between Tripoli or Benghazi and Jeddah, they said.

The sanctions committee allowed EgyptAir to fly Libyan pilgrims to Saudi Arabia in both of the two previous years. Libya symbolically made one pilgrim flight in 1995 and another in 1996 despite the U.N. ban.
Libya also violated the U.N. ban when a Libyan-registered plane flew Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi to Cairo to attend an Arab summit in June 1996.

Last month, it flew an official delegation to Ghana's capital Accra. It told the Security Council that it considered itself no longer subject to the air embargo after it gave permission for an American-piloted balloon to overfly its territory.
JANA did not say when the pilgrim flights would start this year. Moslem pilgrims from all over the world are expected to start flying to Saudi Arabia by the end of March and early April.
